structured_output.draft:
After an update, a familiar setting may be somewhere else, under a new name, or both. The control still exists, but its legibility has been damaged. That matters because software is not a sealed object: its meaning depends partly on whether people can find and understand the choices it offers.

Legibility is a condition of meaningful control. A setting that governs notifications, location access, or account visibility has consequences beyond its label (including consequences for people who did not choose the update). When an update moves the setting, a user can’t reliably tell whether the option was removed, renamed, or simply relocated. When the name changes, the problem is sharper: a familiar instruction may become an unfamiliar phrase, even though the underlying decision remains the same.

This is not merely a matter of convenience. Settings are the points where software becomes accountable to the people using it. If a control is difficult to locate, the practical choice may belong to the interface rather than the person. If a control is renamed without a clear connection to its former meaning, people may accept a change they would have rejected had the choice remained legible. The screen becomes a kind of locked room—full of controls, but difficult to enter on equal terms.

We should therefore expect updates to preserve recognizable names and locations, or explain plainly when either must change. A brief notice can identify the old setting, the new setting, and the effect of the change (a privacy choice deserves especially clear treatment). The standard should be understandable continuity, with limited exceptions for genuine redesigns (and a visible path back to the relevant control).

Software will change. That is ordinary. What should remain ordinary, too, is the ability to see what changed and act on it. A setting can’t be meaningfully available when its path is obscured—legibility is part of control, not decoration.
